title: Rain Day and Weather Delay Pay: What Contractors Owe Their Crews
summary: What contractors owe crews during rain days and weather delays. Covers FLSA rules, reporting time pay, exempt vs. hourly, union provisions, and overtime.
body_markdown:
Rain shuts down a pour. Wind stops a crane pick. Snow closes a road to the site. Weather delays are part of construction, but fewer contractors handle the payroll side well.


No single federal rule governs weather delay pay. The answer depends on whether workers are hourly or salaried, whether they showed up before the call was made, what state the project is in, and whether a[prevailing wage](https://www.buildtrayd.com/blog/what-is-prevailing-wage-davis-bacon-guide) or union agreement applies.


## **What the FLSA Requires**


Federal law draws a hard line between exempt and non-exempt workers, and that classification sets your baseline obligation.


### **Hourly (Non-Exempt) Workers**


Under the FLSA, hourly employees are paid for hours actually worked. If a crew works two hours before getting sent home, you owe two hours. Cancel the shift before anyone reports, and you owe nothing under federal law.


The critical question is waiting time. If workers are on site and told to stand by, that time is generally compensable. They're under your control, unable to use the time freely. Once you release them, the clock stops.


### **Salaried (Exempt) Workers**


To maintain exempt status, you must pay the full weekly salary if an employee works any part of the week. You can deduct for full-day weather absences, but you cannot dock partial days. If the closure lasts the entire workweek and no work is performed, you can withhold pay.


## **Reporting Time Pay: The State Layer**


Federal law doesn't require pay for hourly workers who show up and get sent home. But several states do.


### **States with Reporting Time Requirements**


Reporting time pay (show-up pay) requires employers to pay a minimum number of hours when a worker reports as scheduled and gets less work than expected. States with these laws include California, Connecticut, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, Rhode Island, and DC.


California requires half the scheduled shift (minimum 2 hours, maximum 4). New York requires 4 hours at minimum wage. Massachusetts requires 3 hours. New Jersey requires 1 hour.


### **How This Applies on a Construction Site**


If your crew is scheduled for 8 hours in California and you send them home after 1 hour, you owe 4. In New York, a worker sent home immediately still gets 4 hours at minimum wage.


Some states include exceptions for weather beyond the employer's control, but the language varies. California's "acts of God" exception is narrow and has been litigated. Don't assume it applies to a rainy Tuesday.


## **Union Contracts and Weather Days**


[Union CBAs](https://www.buildtrayd.com/blog/union-payroll-guide-for-trade-contractors) typically address weather delays directly, and their terms override statutory minimums when more generous.


### **Common CBA Provisions**


Many agreements guarantee a minimum call-out (typically 2 to 4 hours) for workers who report. Some define weather thresholds that trigger a paid stoppage versus an unpaid send-home.


### **Why the CBA Governs**


On[union projects](https://www.buildtrayd.com/solution/compliance/union-payroll) , CBA terms are contractual obligations. Sending a crew home without the guaranteed minimum triggers a grievance. Different trades on the same project may have different guarantees.


## **Prevailing Wage and Certified Payroll Implications**


Weather delays add a reporting layer on prevailing wage projects that's often overlooked.


### **Waiting Time at Prevailing Rates**


If workers on a Davis-Bacon or[state prevailing wage](https://www.buildtrayd.com/blog/state-prevailing-wage-laws-contractors) project are on site and required to wait, those hours must be paid at the applicable[prevailing rate](https://www.buildtrayd.com/blog/how-to-calculate-prevailing-wage-fringe-benefits) , including fringes.


### **Certified Payroll Reporting**


Compensable delay hours must appear on[certified payroll reports](https://www.buildtrayd.com/products/payroll/construction-payroll-reports) . Omitting them from[certified payroll](https://www.buildtrayd.com/blog/what-is-certified-payroll-contractor-guide) creates discrepancies in compliance filings. Track them separately so they don't distort production totals.


## **Overtime After Weather Delays**


The bigger payroll risk is when makeup hours push into[overtime](https://www.buildtrayd.com/blog/construction-overtime-rules-federal-state-prevailing-wage) .


### **Catch-Up Work and the 40-Hour Week**


A crew that loses Monday to rain and works 10-hour days Tuesday through Saturday hits 50 hours, with 10 at overtime. On prevailing wage projects,[overtime applies](https://www.buildtrayd.com/products/payroll/construction-payroll) to the base rate only, with fringes at straight time on every hour. In daily overtime states (California, Alaska, Nevada), overtime triggers after 8 hours each day regardless of weekly totals.


### **Show-Up Pay and Overtime**


In states with reporting time pay, those paid-but-not-worked hours generally don't count toward the 40-hour overtime threshold. Check your state's rules.


## **Where Contractors Get It Wrong**


Weather is unpredictable. Pay obligations don't have to be.


### **No Written Weather Policy**


Without a policy, every superintendent makes their own call. One sends crews home at the first drop; another waits two hours. Payroll processes both the same way, and neither matches what the state or CBA requires.


### **Not Tracking Delay Hours Separately**


Lumping delay time into regular hours inflates job costs. Tracking it as unpaid when compensable creates wage exposure. Use your[time tracking system](https://www.buildtrayd.com/products/field/foreman-app) to record when work stopped, when it resumed, and whether workers were released or held.


### **Ignoring Multi-State Rules**


A contractor with crews in California and Texas faces two different obligations. California requires show-up pay; Texas does not. The same policy across both means overpaying in one or underpaying in the other.

## **FAQs**


### Do construction workers get paid when it rains?


It depends. Hourly workers are generally paid only for hours worked under the FLSA, but state reporting time laws may require minimum pay if a worker shows up and is sent home. Union contracts often guarantee minimum call-out hours. Salaried exempt employees must receive their full weekly salary if they work any part of the week.


### What is reporting time pay?


Reporting time pay (or show-up pay) is a state law requiring employers to pay a minimum number of hours when a worker reports as scheduled and gets less work than expected. States with these laws include California, New York, Massachusetts, New Jersey, and others. Requirements range from 1 to 4 hours depending on the state.


### Does weather delay time count toward overtime?


Paid weather delay hours may or may not count toward the 40-hour overtime threshold depending on your state and whether the hours are classified as worked or reporting time pay. Makeup hours after weather delays frequently push workers into overtime, which must be calculated correctly on prevailing wage projects.


### How should contractors track weather delay hours?


Record when work stopped, when it resumed, and whether workers were released or held on site. Track delay hours as a separate category so they appear correctly in payroll and certified payroll reports without inflating production-hour totals.


### Do union contracts require rain day pay?


Many union CBAs guarantee a minimum call-out (typically 2 to 4 hours) when workers report to the site. Some include specific weather thresholds. The terms vary by trade and local, so review each applicable agreement before setting a weather policy.


*This guide is for informational purposes only. Weather delay pay obligations vary by state, contract, union agreement, and project type. Consult your legal and compliance teams for requirements specific to your situation.*
